<meta>continues from previous page: this text translates commentaries on Chapter 48 and the beginning of Chapter 49 of the Tao Te Ching</meta>

<margin>Su’s Commentary <note>Su Zhe, 1039 to 1112, a prominent Song dynasty official and scholar</note></margin>Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but devote themselves to learning find that what they hear and see increases daily. Because they have nothing to unify these observations, these things inevitably become a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it. This is the second level of knowledge." If one day a person knows the Way and looks back at their past artificial actions, they will see that every single one was a delusion. To remove delusion and return to one's true nature is what is meant by "reduction." Confucius said to Zigong: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with one principle." Removing delusion to seek a return to nature can be called reduction, yet the mind that seeks to remove delusion still remains. Once one forgets even this mind, and pure nature remains with nothing else, then whatever one does will not fail to align with <term>wu wei</term> <gloss>non-action or effortless action</gloss>. All people have desires and a mind that wishes to grasp the affairs and principles of the world. Therefore, they create trouble by seeking things; their intentions are visible externally and so things resist them, and in the end, they gain nothing. The Sage practices non-action and thus his mind is without "affairs." His intentions are not visible externally and things are at peace with him. Although he does not try to grasp or act upon the affairs of the world, all affairs and principles under heaven follow him and find peace.

<margin>Lü’s Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032 to 1111, a Song dynasty politician and commentator</note></margin>Those who practice learning are those who have not yet heard the Way. Since they seek what they have not heard, they must be broad in their pursuit; thus they increase daily. Those who practice the Way are those who have already heard it. Since they have heard it and practice it, they aim only for non-action; thus they reduce daily. This reduction is still not free from "doing." Only when one reduces even the act of reducing does one reach non-action. Non-action means being still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" means that when stimulated, one penetrates all the causes under heaven. Practicing the Way to this point is called "the end of learning, free from worry." It is called "the spirit has no fixed direction and the Changes have no physical form." Unless one is the most divine person under heaven, who could achieve this? From this perspective, one always takes the world through non-action. Once one resorts to "having affairs" <note>willful action</note>, it is clear that one is not sufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai’s Commentary <note>Huang Maocai, a Southern Song dynasty scholar</note></margin>Only after one knows everything can one speak of "learning." Thus, learning desires daily increase. Only after that which was increased has been transformed can one speak of the "Way." Thus, the Way desires daily reduction. What is increased can be sought through progress, but what is reduced is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only those with ultimate clarity can suddenly let everything drop away and reach the realm of non-action. Thus they can leave nothing undone, and their practical application is inexhaustible. Their influence spreads across the world with ample room to spare.

<margin>Xizhai’s Commentary <note>Li Daochun, a 13th century Taoist master whose literary name was Xizhai</note></margin>Practicing learning is the means to seek knowledge, so it increases daily. Practicing the Way is the means to remove delusion, so it reduces daily. If knowledge is not perfected, then reduction will not be complete; therefore, daily increase is the foundation for daily reduction. If one reduces and further reduces until delusion is gone and truth is complete, then there is non-action. Upon reaching non-action, even in "doing," there is nothing that is not "non-doing." This state cannot easily be discussed in terms of increase or reduction. When non-action reaches its peak, though the world is vast, one unifies it with a single principle. If one uses "affairs" to give rise to more "affairs," then even a single object before one's eyes will become entangled and confused, let alone the vastness of the world.

The Sage has no fixed heart <note>or mind</note>; he takes the heart of the people as his own. To those who are good, I am good. To those who are not good, I am also good; thus virtue is goodness. To those who are trustful, I trust them. To those who are not trustful, I also trust them; thus virtue is trust. The Sage is cautious in the world; for the sake of the world, he keeps his heart undifferentiated. The people all focus their ears and eyes on him; the Sage <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page</note>

<summary>This page contains four commentaries on the Tao Te Ching regarding the difference between accumulating knowledge and practicing the Way through reduction. It also begins Chapter 49, describing how the Sage adopts the hearts of the people as his own.</summary>
<keywords>Laozi, Tao Te Ching, wu wei, non-action, reduction, learning, Su Zhe, Lü Huiqing, virtue, Sage</keywords>
